overview.text: This Draft Alternatives Analysis/EIS/EIR evaluates eleven transit alternatives—five rail rapid transit/bus options, five all-bus options, and a 'Null' no-build option—to improve transit service in the approximately 55-square-mile Los Angeles Regional Core. The Regional Core is the densest part of the Los Angeles urbanized area, containing 600,000 residents and 542,000 jobs across six community plan areas including Central City, Westlake, Wilshire, Hollywood, Sherman Oaks-Studio City, and North Hollywood. Alternatives range from an 18-mile rail line through Wilshire-Fairfax to North Hollywood (the highest-patronage option) to aerial busways, exclusive bus lanes, TSM improvements, and a no-build base case. Environmental consequences include long-term regional air quality improvement and energy savings under rail alternatives, but also significant displacement (78 to 723 structures under cut-and-cover/aerial), seismic risks from the San Andreas and Newport-Inglewood faults, and severe traffic and business impacts from surface bus lane alternatives. Four rounds of community meetings revealed general public preference for rail over bus, strong opposition to cut-and-cover construction and exclusive bus lanes, and interest in proceeding with a starter line without new taxes.

project_description.text: This Draft Alternatives Analysis/EIS/EIR evaluates eleven transit alternatives to improve transit service in the approximately 55-square-mile Los Angeles Regional Core. The eleven alternatives include five rail rapid transit/bus options, five all-bus options ranging from an exclusive aerial busway to surface lane reservations, and a 'Null' no-build option. The system is Element IV of the Regional Transit Development Program, with rail alternatives ranging from 8 to 18 miles and serving the LACBD and Union Station. Capital costs in 1977 dollars range from $659 million (Alt. V) to $1,450 million (Alt. VI).

affected_community.text: The Regional Core is the densest part of the Los Angeles urbanized area, containing 600,000 residents (21% of City total) and 542,000 jobs (43% of City total) across six community plan areas: Central City, Westlake, Wilshire, Hollywood, Sherman Oaks-Studio City, and North Hollywood. The area ranks third among U.S. urbanized areas in population density, with 41.2% minority population and current Regional Core transit mode split of about 12%, much higher than the 3.4% SCAG regional average. The corridor includes nineteen educational institutions, seven libraries, eight major medical facilities, and major ethnic communities such as Chinatown and Little Tokyo. Lower-income areas like Westlake-Central City have median household income 32% below the citywide average.

alternatives_overview.text: Eleven alternatives are evaluated: five Rail Rapid Transit/Bus options (I–V) ranging from 8 to 18 miles, all serving the LACBD and varying through Wilshire to La Brea, Fairfax, or Vermont and onward to Hollywood/North Hollywood; an aerial busway (VI); three exclusive bus lane options (VII–IX) using median or curb lanes on Wilshire/La Brea or 8th/Olympic; a TSM bus improvement option (X); and a 'Null' Alternative XI representing no change. Rail alternatives can be configured as bored subway, cut-and-cover, or aerial. Alternative II, an 18-mile rail line, yields the highest patronage at 275,000 boardings, while All-Bus Alternatives VII-X can be implemented within five years versus seven to eight years for rail/aerial busway. The selection was limited to rail rapid transit and bus modes per a 1976 Secretary of Transportation directive.

environmental_impact.text: Long-term air quality would improve under transit improvement alternatives (I–X) versus the Null due to reduced vehicle travel, with rail Alternative II saving up to 100,000 daily auto trips and 710,000 VMT, though regional improvement is only about 0.1%. Rail/Bus alternatives would save 29,000-44,000 equivalent barrels of oil per year, while All-Bus alternatives VII-X would use 28,000-39,000 more EBOs annually than the Null. Cut-and-cover and aerial configurations would displace 78 to 723 structures, and aerial guideways pose visual, shadow, and noise impacts—particularly to MacArthur Park, Hancock Park, Barnsdall Park, and sound-sensitive medical centers. Seismic risks include strong shaking from the San Andreas (Magnitude 8.5 maximum credible) and Newport-Inglewood (Magnitude 7.5) faults, with potential liquefaction and oil/gas/hydrogen sulphide seeps near the La Brea Tar Pits. Surface bus alternatives VII-IX would cause severe traffic congestion and adverse impacts on businesses by eliminating curb parking on Wilshire and La Brea.

public_response.text: Over fourteen months four rounds of community meetings, organization meetings, and media briefings were conducted throughout the Regional Core by Los Angeles City Planning staff with SCRTD assistance, with close liaison maintained with the Los Angeles City Council's Transportation Committee and the LACTC Citizens Advisory Committee. Participants generally favored rail over bus at this stage, with adamant opposition to cut-and-cover subway construction and concerns about earthquake dangers. Businesses opposed exclusive bus lanes due to negative business impacts, while residents raised concerns about funding sources and property taxes, expressing strong interest in proceeding with a rapid transit starter line without new taxes. Hollywood community groups specifically expressed a strong desire for locating the Hollywood station at Cahuenga and Hollywood Boulevards.

value.description: A 16-mile rail rapid transit line running from the Los Angeles CBD along Wilshire to La Brea, then north through Hollywood to a terminal station in North Hollywood, providing service between the San Fernando Valley and the CBD.

themes.justification: The document centers on evaluating eleven transit alternatives (rail and bus) to improve mobility across the Los Angeles Regional Core, directly addressing mobility networks and infrastructure impacts including displacement of 78–723 structures, visual/noise effects, and seismic risks. The dense urban context—600,000 residents, 542,000 jobs, and six community plan areas—grounds the analysis in urban land use, planning, and built environment considerations.
